I'm not a smart man: can you explain what a container does or doesn't. if I see Google this, there are a lot of people happy and also not happy with this Dock development.

Docker is kind of like a slimmed down VM, or a bigger chroot. It allows a process (or processes, but most docker stuff I've heard [which isn't much] suggests one process/application per container) to run in its own space/environment. It doesn't boot is own OS, it uses the host system's kernel/etc. It has it's own disk area, but you can give it access to "shared" spaces too.

The idea is if you have a web application that is scalable, you could deploy a server that runs docker. Then you'd create a docker container that holds your web application. THEN, you fire up an instance of that container to server your application. If it gets busy, you can quickly fire up more instances of that container to handle the load. The containers are meant to be portable, so you can bring that container to another server (even with a different host OS) and fire up more instances on that server. This can give you an advantage over one single server using all it's resources to provide a single application (standard server mode) because it allows you to do upgrades/whatever without downtime. You just slowly take down one of the instances and re-launch it with the updated container. If you do some resource balancing, this will also allow you to share CPU and memory resources between different application servers, with you being able to scale instances up and down automatically (something you would have to provide the smarts for).

It's not super secure though. I think people can break out of the docker 'jail' if they had enough knowledge to.

I am sure others can add more info, but this is Docker how I understand it. I can see the appeal in some situations, but not in others, so I understand why people are on either side of the fence about it.
Thanks for your explanation. It helps the plebs like me :)
